item.title: Gaza: ‘She survived the bombing, but not the blockade’
item.description:
Gaza: ‘She survived the bombing, but not the blockade’

After two years of bombardment and forced displacement during Israel’s genocide in Gaza, Suhaila al-Mabhouh had one wish: to go home.

The 60-year-old Palestinian longed so desperately to return to her family home in northern Gaza that she turned down an evacuation offer to Italy, submitted by her daughter, who lives there.

When the so-called ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025, she and her husband rushed back to their home in Jabalia refugee camp.

She began making small repairs to the badly damaged house, hoping to piece her life back together after two years of bombardment.

But the hope of rebuilding was short-lived, as Israel maintained its siege and continued its daily bombardment.

Read more: Gaza: ‘She survived the bombing, but not the blockade’

item.title: Palestinian succumbs to wounds sustained in Israeli attack in northern Gaza
item.description:
Palestinian succumbs to wounds sustained in Israeli attack in northern Gaza

A Palestinian man has died from wounds sustained in an Israeli attack in northern Gaza, Wafa news agency reports, citing medical sources.

According to the sources, Khaled Abdel-Fattah Jaber, died from wounds sustained in an Israeli drone strike on Sunday.

In a separate attack, another Palestinian was wounded by Israeli fire near Abu Hamid Roundabout, east of Khan Younis city in Gaza's south.

Al Jazeera reports that Jaber's death brings the total number of people killed in Gaza on Monday to three, with two others killed in a drone attack in Rafah.

According to Gaza's health ministry Israel has killed at least 1,493 and wounded another 5,299 since the so-called ceasefire was implemented a year ago.

item.title: Israeli elections: Grotesque court spectacle sets a chilling precedent
item.description:
Israeli elections: Grotesque court spectacle sets a chilling precedent

Submitted by Orly Noy on Thu, 10/08/2026 - 20:05
Ruling to uphold the disqualification of Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh shows the true face of our 'democracy'
Sami Abu Shehadeh, pictured at centre, and other Arab politicians attend a hearing at the Supreme Court in Jerusalem, on 1 October 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off

If Israel still had any masks left to conceal the depths of its anti-democratic descent, they were shattered in the Supreme Court last week, when an expanded panel of nine justices heard petitions seeking to disqualify all Arab lists from running for the Knesset, as well as two individual candidates: Hadash MK Ofer Cassif and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh.

It is a ritual repeated in every Israeli election: the Central Elections Committee, a political body dominated by the governing coalition, broadly disqualifies Arab parties and individual candidates. The Supreme Court then overturns those decisions in order to preserve Israel’s image as a democratic state. 

This time, in a profoundly dangerous precedent, the court did not overturn the committee’s decision regarding Abu Shehadeh, and upheld his disqualification from running for parliament. 

This was not the only red line crossed. Under Israeli law, an individual or a list can be disqualified from running for the Knesset on several grounds, including rejecting Israel’s character as a Jewish and democratic state, and supporting armed struggle against the state. 

Because the first could theoretically be used not only to disqualify Arab parties, but also non-Zionist ultra-Orthodox parties, the court has over the years found ways around this obstacle.

As for supporting armed struggle, right-wing parties have long invested enormous resources in trying to pin this accusation on Arab parties and representatives. Every statement made by a Palestinian candidate over the years, every article they have written, every social-media post or event they have attended - all are examined under a magnifying glass, in hopes of somehow proving such support. 

This time, the “trophy” they found was an article by Abu Shehadeh published in Arabic on 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attack, offering an initial analysis of the event and the reality that had emerged.

Broad support

The petition to disqualify Abu Shehadeh on the basis of that article was filed by National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, the ideological descendant of Meir Kahane, whose own movement was declared a terrorist organisation and outlawed in 1994 after the Ibrahimi Mosque massacre, carried out by Kahanist Baruch Goldstein. 

The fact that the disqualification petition was filed by Ben Gvir - a man convicted of supporting a terrorist organisation, who had a framed photograph of the mass murderer Goldstein in his living room, and who celebrated his most recent birthday with a cake bearing a festive image of a noose, which has become his trademark - should alone have been enough for any decent party to reject it.

Yet this is where the first dangerous precedent emerged. Not only was the disqualification petition supported by the Jewish right and centrist opposition parties; it was also backed by the Democrats, led by Yair Golan - the party supposedly representing the Zionist left, which speaks frequently of “Jewish-Arab partnership”. 

Like everything else in the only democracy in the universe, even the right to be morally outraged is a privilege reserved exclusively for Jews

That partnership, it turns out, can easily be tossed into the garbage the moment the Zionist left seeks to prove its loyalty to the other Zionist parties with which it hopes to form the next government. For that purpose, they will not hesitate to throw under the bus a Palestinian leader engaged in a political struggle for justice and equality.

The second precedent set in this case is far more serious and dangerous. For the first time, the Supreme Court did not overturn an entirely political decision by the Central Elections Committee, and instead upheld Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification from running for the Knesset. 

This was despite the objections of a long list of prominent legal scholars, including former Deputy Attorney General Dina Zilber, law professor Barak Medina, academic David Harel, and even attorney Moshe Cohen-Eliya, a law professor associated with the far right, whose own analysis concluded that there was no legal basis for the disqualification. 

But these proceedings had very little, if anything, to do with law. More than anything, the case resembled a Shin Bet interrogation.

I sat in the courtroom, stunned, and watched this disgraceful hearing for more than three hours. The Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party was represented by Ben Gvir himself, and by attorney Ze’ev Wolf, previously convicted of murdering a Palestinian man in Jerusalem’s Old City in November 1992, two years after Rabbi Meir Kahane’s assassination. He was later pardoned.

This is the Jewish and democratic state: two men convicted of terrorism-related offences seeking to silence a Palestinian leader who has devoted his life to a political struggle for equality and justice. They are backed by the entire Zionist spectrum, from right to left, as well as by the Supreme Court itself.

Moral outrage

In a country whose political and military leaders have called for the indiscriminate annihilation of a civilian population and the starvation of more than two million people in Gaza; a country facing proceedings over the commission of genocide, and whose prime minister is the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court; in this country, a Palestinian public leader is given a show trial over an article he wrote.

This is Israeli democracy in all its glory.

There is not enough space here to recount all the miserable absurdities that unfolded during the hearing. But one thing in particular caught my attention: the emotionally charged vocabulary used by the justices and the lawyers on the right. One expression, above all, kept recurring: “disgust”.

Netanyahu won't stop until all Arab political parties are gone
Read More »

They felt disgust at the fairly elementary analysis in Abu Shehadeh’s article, in which he wrote that a pressure cooker eventually explodes, and that the struggle must be redirected towards political channels. They felt disgust at Cassif’s uncompromising solidarity with the oppressed. They felt disgust at Balad’s insistence on genuine equality and substantive democracy for everyone. 

Even I, a candidate ranked 15th on the Joint List for the Knesset, representing Balad, apparently managed to arouse a measure of their disgust because of an article in which I wrote about the obligation to distinguish between combatants and a civilian population.

The genocide in Gaza, with its tens of thousands of victims and two million people starved and dehydrated, many of whom have been orphaned, maimed and displaced, needless to say, did not arouse their disgust.

The Palestinians sitting in the courtroom, stone-faced as they watched this grotesque spectacle unfold, expressed no disgust.

Perhaps their souls, crushed day after day beneath the wheels of Jewish supremacy, are simply too exhausted to feel disgust anymore. Or perhaps they know all too well that, like everything else in the only democracy in the universe, even the right to be morally outraged is a privilege reserved exclusively for Jews.

From uneasy partners to open distrust: Aoun and Hezbollah struggle to rebuild ties
item.description:
From uneasy partners to open distrust: Aoun and Hezbollah struggle to rebuild ties

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:21
Restoring relations between Lebanon's president and Hezbollah will require much more than reopening channels of communication
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the Presidential Palace in Baabda, Lebanon, 15 September 2026 (Joseph Eid/AFP)
Off

The relationship between Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Hezbollah has deteriorated into a dispute over weapons, sovereignty and the future of Lebanon’s security, with sources on both sides acknowledging that communication continues but trust has largely collapsed.

When Aoun was elected president in January 2025, Hezbollah supported his election, helping end a prolonged presidential vacancy. But the political understanding that facilitated his election did not resolve the fundamental disagreement over Hezbollah’s independent military structure and the state’s authority to decide matters of war and peace.

From the beginning of his presidency, Aoun made clear that he wanted weapons brought under state control. In his inaugural address, he pledged to affirm the state’s right to monopolise arms, linking the principle to strengthening the Lebanese Armed Forces, protecting the country’s borders and implementing international resolutions.

His position became more explicit in a speech marking Army Day in July 2025, when he called for the army and security forces to have the exclusive right to bear arms, urging Hezbollah and its supporters to “place your bet solely on the Lebanese state”.

The disagreement deepened in January 2026, when Aoun said the circumstances that had once justified weapons outside state control no longer existed, and that their continued presence had become a burden on Hezbollah’s own community and Lebanon as a whole.

Hezbollah criticised the remarks, expressing “disappointment” with Aoun’s position.

Party spokesperson Youssef al-Zein argued that Hezbollah was exercising restraint in the face of Israeli attacks and that further disarmament should not be discussed before Israel withdrew from positions it continued to occupy in southern Lebanon.

The dispute extended beyond disarmament.

In late January, Hezbollah's leader Naim Qassem said the party was “not neutral” in a potential conflict involving the United States and Iran. The presidency reiterated that decisions on war and peace belonged to the Lebanese state, underscoring the tension between Hezbollah’s regional commitments and Aoun’s insistence that such decisions be made by state institutions.

The decisive rupture came on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel following the US-Israeli assassination of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

The government responded by banning Hezbollah’s military and security activities, calling on the group to surrender its weapons and directing the army to advance its plan to bring all weapons under state control north of the Litani River. Aoun condemned the rocket launch, further straining relations with the party that had supported his election.

'Aoun 1, Aoun 2'

A source close to Hezbollah said trust in the presidency had been exhausted, citing what the source described as Aoun’s failure to honour previous understandings and his support for the government’s response.

“The first step is to reverse the decision,” the source said, arguing that normal engagement was impossible while Hezbollah’s military and security activities remained banned. The source also accused Aoun of placing excessive faith in Washington, saying he appeared to believe that meeting US President Donald Trump had made the United States his ally.

The source offered a pointed assessment of the president’s transformation: “You could say there is Joseph Aoun 1, the army commander, and a different Joseph Aoun 2, the president. The first is not like the second.”

South Lebanon: 'It's torture, they are razing our lives before our eyes'
Read More »

The presidency disputes Hezbollah’s account of the relationship. A source close to Baabda said ties had not been severed, but remained below the level required given the sensitivity of the current period. Communication continued through an established channel, the source said, but there had been no return to high-level engagement.

“Nothing” prevents direct communication from the presidency’s side, the source said, adding that Hezbollah’s demands were unrealistic under the current circumstances.

The source also said that attempts to communicate with Hezbollah had been made on several occasions, but questioned who was making decisions within the organisation.

“To be frank, we do not know who is leading the party today, or whether they themselves even know who actually makes the decisions within Hezbollah,” the source said.

The competing accounts reveal a relationship in which both sides believe the other must make the first move. Hezbollah wants the government to reverse its March decision before trust can be restored, while the presidency maintains that state authority over weapons and decisions of war and peace cannot be negotiable.

The deeper question is whether the two sides can agree on a security arrangement that places decisions firmly in the hands of the Lebanese state while addressing Hezbollah’s argument that its weapons remain necessary in the face of Israeli occupation and attacks.

For now, neither side describes relations as formally severed. But the gap between their positions, and the distrust expressed by sources close to both, suggests that restoring ties will require more than reopening a channel of communication. It will require agreement on the limits of Hezbollah’s military role and the authority of the Lebanese state.
